abstract: Objective Biomarkers of disease pathogenesis are critically needed for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) to facilitate diagnosis and patient stratification into appropriate therapeutic trials. Proteomic studies offer significant potential to advance this, but reproducibility across laboratories is a key component toward identifying protein changes that can be translated into clinical applications. Methods A combined analysis of 25 proteomic studies in human ALS biospecimens was performed to identify proteins consistently altered in ALS postmortem tissue, cerebrospinal fluid, or blood, as well as across primary regions of ALS pathology and peripheral biofluids. We consolidated these datasets into a user‐friendly database “FindMND Biomarker,” which is an accessible search tool that allows users to quickly determine how often, and in which biospecimen types, their proteins of interest are dysregulated in patients with ALS. Results Our combined analysis identified 1,458 altered proteins in ALS, and revealed consistent dysregulation in mitochondrial, cytoplasmic, and RNA binding proteins in primary and later affected regions of ALS pathology. Remarkable consistency in the direction and dysregulation of chitinases and gelsolin proteins were observed across ALS biofluids. Comparisons of postmortem tissue and biofluids reinforce several known protein changes, and highlighted novel proteins of interest that may drive disease pathogenesis. Interpretation The biospecimen type in which protein dysregulation is most consistently identified provides important insight into disease, and whether these represent potential measures of disease pathogenesis or systemic changes. By streamlining proteins by reproducibility and biospecimen type, FindMNDBiomarker is a useful resource that provides new mechanistic insights, and facilitates the prioritization of ALS‐associated proteins for further validation and investigation. ANN NEUROL 2025;98:788–800

The search results were then filtered by 2 independent reviewers to identify and include proteomic studies in human postmortem tissue, CSF, or blood. These included proteomic assessments performed in bulk tissue homogenate, single‐cell motor neurons captured using laser microdissection

CSF,

Studies that did not provide proteomic datasets, including significance values and log fold changes for pairwise comparisons, or that involved cohorts with <3 ALS cases were excluded. Institutional review board approval was not required, because this study utilized publicly available published data.
Proteome Dataset Consolidation and Comparison
Published lists of proteins were manually filtered, and proteins were considered to be differentially expressed if they met at least 1 of the following statistical criteria: Benjamin–Hochberg false discovery rate correction of <5%,
p
< 0.05 using ANOVA followed by post‐hoc analyses, or a combination of
p

To enable comparison between studies, UniProt IDs were collected for each DEP, and >1 ID was provided, the first listed was used. Duplicate proteins within a dataset, isoforms, or uncharacterized proteins were removed.
FindMNDBiomarker
Database
DEPs from each study were uploaded into the FindMNDBiomarker Database (
https://find-mnd-biomarker.sydney.edu.au
), where proteins of interest can be searched for by UniProt ID or biomarker (gene) name, and this will reveal all publications and biospecimen types in which these proteins of interest emerged as significantly dysregulated in the disease group compared with the comparator group (eg, ALS/control or ALS‐fast/ALS‐slow). The cohort sizes, average age at disease onset, collection, and postmortem interval were included in these studies, as well as whether the DEP was upregulated or downregulated in each of these studies and sample types was also included. This database will be actively maintained and updated every 6 months to incorporate datasets from newly published proteomic studies.
Comparison of Protein Changes Within and Across Biospecimens and Cohorts
To identify proteins that were repeatedly significantly dysregulated in cohorts of ALS compared with controls, DEPs identified in studies of the same biospecimen type, as well as in studies of different biospecimens types (postmortem tissue, CSF, blood), were compared. DEPs identified in primary brain regions of ALS pathology (motor cortex, spinal cord) were also compared with DEPs identified in less affected brain regions (frontal cortex). To identify proteins associated with specific ALS subtypes, as well as ALS, studies comparing ALS subtypes without a control cohort were compared with each other. Given that there were few studies of ALS subtypes, DEPs identified between ALS subtypes were also overlapped with our combined analysis, identifying DEPs that overlapped with ≥2 studies of ALS compared with controls. Finally, each protein was ranked by the number of times reported to be significantly dysregulated in these studies in human ALS.
Gene Ontology Analysis
Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis was conducted using g:Profiler.
11
GO terms were filtered to a false discovery rate <0.05, and the full list of proteins identified in ALS compared with controls used as the custom background list (1,458 proteins).
body:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), also known as motor neuron disease (MND), is a rapidly progressive and debilitating neurodegenerative disease with a median survival of ~3 years.
1
An initial misdiagnosis is common, and the lack of an accessible biomarker of disease pathogenesis remains a major limitation for early diagnosis, intervention, and drug development.
2
Proteomic studies have significantly advanced mechanistic understanding of ALS and enabled the discovery of TDP‐43,
3
which is now recognized to be a key pathological driver in almost all patients.
4
However, the development of biomarkers specific to pathological TDP‐43 remains an unsolved challenge. As such, neurofilament light chain, which is a general measure of neurodegeneration‐induced axonal damage, remains the current most promising marker, despite having a limited role in independently distinguishing ALS or outperforming clinical observation.
5
The past few years have witnessed an increasing number of proteomic discovery studies performed in human ALS biospecimens, each providing cross‐sectional insight into underlying disease mechanisms or identifying potential biomarker candidates of these changes. However, when analyzed in isolation, each of these studies remains limited by their low sample size, single biospecimen type, or stage of disease. Reproducibility of ALS‐associated proteins identified across different laboratories is critical to validate and identify promising targets and biomarkers that can be easily utilized in various primary care settings and drug trials. However, the consistency of these proteomic findings across different laboratories, platforms, and cohorts has not been established, hampering the selection of high‐confidence proteins on which to focus targeted and large‐scale validation efforts on. Further to this, whether proteomic findings in patient biofluids are consistent with that in the brain and spinal regions of ALS pathogenesis remain to be established. This is an important consideration, because the biospecimen type in which protein dysregulation is most consistently identified provides insight into whether these represent potential measures of disease pathogenesis or systemic changes that may better reflect clinical disease/progression.
With these considerations, the aim of the present study was to perform a combined analysis of proteomic datasets from ALS postmortem tissue, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and blood to gain a comprehensive overview of the proteins that are consistently altered within these different biospecimen types, as well as across both peripheral biofluids and tissue from primary regions of ALS pathology. Data were consolidated into a user‐friendly online search tool, “FindMNDBiomarker,” to enable users to quickly determine the consistency and biospecimen type in which their proteins of interest have been identified as dysregulated in ALS. We demonstrate the utility of this database in exploring emerging questions and recent advances in the ALS field, including cryptic peptides, extracellular vesicles, and multiplex proteomics.

Results
In total, 25 publications met the study inclusion criteria, encompassing 28 datasets, including 22 proteomic analyses of ALS compared with controls (Table
1
) and 6 analyses of ALS subtypes without a control cohort (Table
2
). Of the 22 proteomic analyses in ALS compared with controls, 7 were in postmortem brain tissue, 10 in CSF, and 5 in plasma or serum samples, encompassing 558 ALS and 384 control cases, and resulting in the identification of 1,458 significantly altered proteins (Fig
1
). Comparisons of ALS subtypes without a control cohort were in biofluids only, and included 2 in rapid versus slower progressing disease (1 in CSF, 1 in plasma); 2 in bulbar versus limb onset ALS (1 in CSF, 1 in plasma/PBMC); 2 comparing early‐ versus late‐stage of disease onset (1 in PMBC, 1 in plasma); and 1 study comparing symptomatic and asymptomatic
C9orf72
carriers (CSF; Table
2
). All DEPs were uploaded to the FindMNDBiomarker Database (Fig
1
).

Studies comparing ALS subtypes without a control cohort included 2 in rapid versus slower progressing disease, 2 in bulbar versus limb onset ALS, 2 in early‐ versus late‐stage of disease onset, and 1 study in symptomatic versus asymptomatic

Protein Changes Identified in Independent Studies of
ALS
Compared with Controls
Postmortem Tissue
The 7 proteomic analyses in postmortem tissue included 3 in bulk tissue homogenate from the spinal cord, 1 single‐cell analysis of lower motor neurons, 2 in bulk frontal tissue, and 1 in extracellular vesicles derived from the motor cortex (Table
1
), collectively identifying 1,015 DEPs. Of the 812 DEPs identified in a primary region of ALS pathology (motor cortex or spinal cord), 64% were decreased (enriched for cytoplasmic translation, RNA binding, and ribosomal proteins), 32% were increased (enriched for cell adhesion, actin cytoskeletal, cadherin binding proteins), and 3% were inconsistently dysregulated (enriched for RNA binding proteins). Of the 258 DEPs in a relatively unaffected region of ALS pathology (frontal cortex), 57% were increased (enriched for proteins involved in aerobic respiration and transmembrane transporter activity), and 43% decreased (enriched for protein binding and cytoplasmic translation).
CSF
Of the 327 DEPs identified in ALS CSF, 59% were increased (enriched for signaling receptor and protein binding), 39% were decreased (enriched for cell adhesion molecule and signaling receptor binding), and 2% (enriched for proteins involved in stress and inflammatory response) were inconsistently dysregulated across studies.
Blood
Of the 116 DEPs identified across five proteomic studies in ALS blood, 55% were increased (enriched for complement activation and peptidase regulator activity), and 45% were decreased (enriched for signal receptor binding).
Protein Changes Consistently Identified Across Independent Studies of
ALS
Compared to Controls (Fig 2A)

DEPs were overlapped, yielding a core list of 53 proteins that repeatedly emerged as significantly dysregulated in at least 3 different studies of ALS compared with controls (Fig
2A
). Of these core DEPs, 23% were repeatedly identified in ≥3 studies of postmortem tissue, 24% in ≥3 studies of biofluids, and 53% were significantly dysregulated in ≥3 studies of tissue and biofluids. Protein dysregulation was generally in the same direction within the same biospecimen type (Fig
2A
), the main exception being between the spinal cord, which is also a primary region of ALS pathology versus the frontal cortex, which is relatively unaffected in ALS (detailed below).
Postmortem Tissue
A total of 77 DEPs were repeatedly identified in at least 50% of the 4 studies in the spinal cord, which is a primary motor region of ALS pathology. Of these, 73% were consistently decreased, and the 27% were consistently increased. Only 2 DEPs identified in motor cortex extracellular vesicles (EVs) were found to overlap, albeit in the opposite direction, with DEPs identified in bulk spinal tissue (DYNC1I1, AHNAK).
A total of 55 DEPs were consistently identified in both a primary region of ALS pathology (motor cortex or spinal tissue) and a less affected brain region (frontal cortex; Supporting Information
S1
). Of these shared DEPs, 25% were dysregulated in the same direction and enriched for RNA binding proteins, 9 of which were highly interconnected RNA binding and ribosomal proteins (SRSF1, SNRPE, EIF5A, KTN1, RPS2, RPS3A, RSP4X, RPS20, RANGAP1). Of the proteins dysregulated in opposite directions, the 51% that were downregulated in the spinal cord and upregulated in the frontal cortices were enriched for proton transmembrane transport and oxidative phosphorylation, suggesting cellular dyshomeostasis and mitochondrial dysfunction in a primary ALS region, which may lead to compensatory upregulation of these proteins in a later implicated brain region. The remaining 24% proteins that were downregulated in the frontal cortices and upregulated in the spinal cord were enriched for reactive oxygen species metabolic process and protein polymerization, suggesting that oxidative stress and protein misfolding or aggregation is an early event leading to compensatory upregulation to meet increased energy demand.
12
CSF
A total of 26 DEPs were repeatedly identified in ≥2 different cohorts, and only 9 DEPs repeatedly identified across a minimum of 3 different studies (NEFM, CHI3L1, CHIT1, CHI3L2, APOB, APP, FUCA2, SERPINA3, UCHL1). Of these, only 5 DEPs were consistently upregulated across >40% (4/9) different cohorts (NEFM, CHIT1, CHI3L1, CHI3L2, UCHL1). With the exception of only 2 proteins (SERPINA3, C1QC) that emerged as significantly dysregulated in the 1 study of CSF exosome‐enriched fractions, and at least 1 study of CSF, no other DEPs were shared between enriched and non‐enriched CSF fractions.
Blood
The 5 proteomic studies in blood included 1 in serum, three in plasma and one in extracellular vesicles derived from plasma (Table
1
). Of the 3 studies in plasma, 1 used aptamer‐based technology (SOMAScan), and the other 2 used mass spectrometry (MS). Interestingly, only 1 shared DEP (CA1) emerged across SOMAScan and MS analyses of the 3 studies in ALS plasma.
Of the DEPs identified in plasma‐derived EVs, 9 were also identified in ALS plasma (C1QC, PROS1, GSN, ORM1, C5, C9, CFI, CPN2, PRG4) and 2 in serum (GSN, EFEMP1), with these proteins dysregulated in the same direction. Gelsolin (GSN) was the only DEP consistently downregulated across different blood components (plasma, serum, plasma‐derived EVs).
Protein Changes Consistently Identified Between Different Biospecimen Types of
ALS
Compared with Controls
Despite the vastly different starting point in biospecimen types analyzed using varying methods by different laboratories, 41 proteins emerged as significantly dysregulated in studies of postmortem tissue and CSF (Fig
2B
). Of these, 4 DEPs were repeatedly identified in at least 4 different studies (NEFH, NEFM, UCHL1, SERPINA3). In contrast, 12 DEPs were shared across postmortem tissue and blood (Fig
2B
). Comparisons of biofluid proteomes identified 13 DEPs shared between CSF and blood, 5 of which (GSN, APOB, C1QC, C5, C9, CFI) were repeatedly identified in at least 4 different studies, and of these, GSN and APOB emerged as consistently dysregulated across 5 different studies of biofluid.
Comparisons of the 3 different biospecimen types (postmortem tissue, CSF, blood) from cohorts analyzed by different laboratories revealed 7 overlapping DEPs in ALS compared to healthy controls (FGA, HBB, C3, HBA, ORM1, CST3, APOD).
Protein Changes Identified in Plasma‐Derived
EVs
and Plasma/Serum
To determine whether plasma‐derived EVs or plasma and serum identify protein changes that overlap with proteins dysregulated in the ALS central nervous system, we compared the DEPs identified in postmortem tissue and CSF with the DEPs identified in either plasma‐derived EVs or plasma and serum samples. This revealed 19 DEPs from plasma‐derived EVs, and 20 DEPs from plasma or serum samples that overlapped with ALS‐associated DEPs in patient tissue and CSF. Only 10 of these DEPs that overlapped with DEPs in postmortem tissues/CSF were shared across plasma‐derived EVs and plasma or serum samples (C1QC, C5, C9, CFI, GSN, ORM1, PROS1, CPN2, EFEMP1, PRG4), indicating the identification of different proteomes in plasma and serum compared with plasma‐derived EVs (Supporting Information
S2
).
Protein Changes Consistently Identified Between
ALS
Subtypes
Two studies compared patients with rapid versus slower progressing disease (ALSFRS‐R scores of >0.7 versus <0.5 units/month). Between these 2 studies in different biofluids (1 in CSF, 1 in plasma), 7 proteins were found to be consistently dysregulated (APOD, BASP1, CFI, CPB2, CPN1, FCN3, TGFBI). We entered these 7 proteins on FindMNDBiomarkers, and identified 6 that had also been identified as DEPs in at least 1 study of ALS compared with controls (APOD, BASP1, CFI, CPB2, FCN3, TGFBI).
Two studies compared patients with limb‐ compared with bulbar‐onset disease, but only 2 DEPs (C6, COTL1) were found to be consistently dysregulated between these 2 studies involving different biofluids (1 CSF, 1 blood).
One study compared
C9ORF72
‐ALS and asymptomatic
C9ORF72
carriers, and found 513 significant protein changes that may occur before transition from asymptomatic to manifest disease. Given that this was the only study of this subtype comparison, we compared these findings with our combined analysis to determine whether these proteins were also affected in symptomatic ALS compared with controls. This revealed 42 proteins that had also been identified as DEPs in at least 2 studies of ALS compared with controls. Of these, the 2 highest ranked proteins were UCHL1 and neurofilament medium chain (NEFM), both having been identified in 6 studies of ALS compared with controls (2 postmortem tissue, 4 biofluid). UCHL1 was recently confirmed to be significantly dysregulated in the CSF of an independent cohort of
C9ORF72
‐ALS compared with asymptomatic
C9ORF72
carriers, which further demonstrated that UCHL1 was also significantly elevated in asymptomatic
C9ORF72
carriers compared with age‐matched non‐carriers.
13
Protein Changes Consistently Identified Across All Human
ALS
Biospecimens
A total of 154 DEPs were identified across all studies in ALS biospecimens (≥3 studies), and of these, the highest confidence proteins identified across all ALS biospecimen types (≥5 studies) were 28 DEPs that included recognized proteins; for example, neurofilament proteins (neurofilament light chain, NEFM), the deubiquitinating enzyme, UCHL1, and chitinases (CHI3L1, CHI3L2, CHIT1); emerging proteins of interest, including the protease inhibitor, SERPINA3, which has also been implicated in blood brain barrier disruption,
14
the glutamate enzymes (GOT1, GOT2), apolipoproteins (APOB, APOD); as well as novel proteins that have been histologically verified to be expressed in healthy spinal motor neurons, but lost in patients with ALS; for example, the mitochondrial protein, ATP5D,
15
and antioxidant protein, PRDX2 (Fig
3
, Table
S3
).

Discussion
The present series performed a combined analysis of proteomic studies across different human ALS biospecimens, identifying the highest confidence protein changes in studies of ALS postmortem tissue, CSF, or blood, as well as between primary regions of ALS pathology and peripheral biofluids. Our study identified a subset of RNA binding and ribosomal proteins that were dysregulated in the same direction across a primary motor region and later affected brain region.
17
,
18
,
19
Dysregulation in RNA binding proteins has been shown to elicit distinct aggregation patterns,
20
and interestingly, of these identified proteins, SRSF1 has been found to suppress TDP‐43 pathology, with its expression levels correlating with cryptic splice junction inclusion to suggest it may be a potential therapeutic target.
21
,
22
,
23
Across series, neurofilament light, medium, and heavy polypeptides (neurofilament light chain, NEFM, neurofilament heavy chain), were consistently decreased in postmortem spinal tissue, but increased in ALS biofluids, supporting that with increasing neuronal death and axonal damage in ALS,
24
neurofilament proteins are released into the extracellular space and increased in biofluids. Interestingly, NEFM, which is relatively less studied, emerged as the most consistently dysregulated neurofilament protein. This converges with a recent finding that NEFM drives discrimination of ALS.
25
An opposing pattern of dysregulation was also seen with UCHL1, which is highly expressed in neurons, and plays a key role in the ubiquitin‐proteasome system,
26
as well as with the neuronal marker, MAP2, which is an early marker of ischemic neuronal damage
27
that decreases with spinal motor neuron loss in ALS.
28
Other proteins significantly dysregulated albeit in the same direction across a primary region of ALS pathology, and biofluids include the protease inhibitor SERPINA3, which has been implicated in blood–brain barrier disruption,
14
calcium‐ and zinc‐binding proteins (S100A6, S100A11), and the glycoprotein, GPNMB. Histological examination has corroborated the increase of some of these proteins, and identified their cellular localization in ALS. For example, increased SERPINA3 has been identified in sporadic ALS cases, where it is predominantly observed in reactive astrocytes
29
; and increased S100A6 has been found to accumulate in pyramidal and lateral corticospinal tracts in sporadic ALS cases.
30
Interestingly, GPNMB has been found to accumulate in spinal motor neurons in ALS, where it aggregates and co‐localizes with pathological TDP‐43, suggesting possible involvement in disease pathogenesis.
31
Several proteins, including the neuronal damage marker, ENO2, and the Golgi‐localized marker, NUCB1, emerged as repeatedly dysregulated in postmortem studies only. Although this may indicate the need for more targeted immunoassays to detect these protein changes in patient biofluids, as is the case with ENO2,
32
the repeat identification of these proteins across postmortem studies suggests prioritizing further investigations into their involvement in disease pathogenesis. Of interest, NUCB1 was recently discovered to be a chaperone‐like amyloid‐binding protein that binds and stabilizes multiple types of amyloid protofibrils,
33
but has yet to be studied in relation to TDP‐43 protofilaments.
34
Contrary to this, several proteins were identified in biofluids only, and may represent systemic changes in ALS. This included the chitinase and chitinase‐like proteins, which are inflammatory markers that have been related to disease progression.
35
The ubiquitously expressed actin‐binding GSN protein plays a key role in cytoskeletal dynamics, and was also consistently identified in 5 biofluid studies of ALS compared with controls.
36
Cryptic exons have been proposed to represent mechanistic readouts of early TDP‐43 dysfunction if reliably detected in biofluids. However, even if cryptic exons escape nonsense‐mediated decay and have highly expressed transcripts, they may require targeted assays (eg. HDGFL2),
37
which can be time‐ and cost‐intensive to develop, and still not be detected in biofluids.
38
Recent studies in TDP‐43‐depleted induced pluripotent stem cells‐derived neurons have further identified expression of various cryptic peptides, a subset of which are present in ALS/FTD CSF,
39
highlighting the need for larger validation studies to determine whether these cryptic peptides are reproducibly dysregulated in ALS. To determine whether these proteins bearing potential cryptic peptides have been implicated in ALS, we entered these canonical proteins into the FindMNDBiomarker search tool. This identified dysregulation of CAMK2B and AGRN in studies of ALS compared with controls, and CAMK2B, SYT7, and AGRN in studies of bulbar‐ compared with limb‐onset ALS, supporting further study of these proteins and their derived peptides. Although shotgun proteomics is likely to lack the sensitivity for low abundant cryptic peptides, this further demonstrates the utility of our search tool as a first pass mechanism that allows users to quickly position their proteins of interest in the context of other studies in ALS biospecimens to help determine whether to prioritize their proteins for further investigation, thereby supporting the target validation pipeline.
Newer proteomic technologies, such as the multiplex affinity‐based SomaScan, have boasted an improved dynamic range in biofluids compared with mass spectrometry. At the time of this review, 1 study had analyzed ALS plasma with SomaScan, and we compared the DEPs identified in this study with the DEPs identified by MS. This revealed only 1 common DEP (carbonic anhydrase I [CA1]) across the 2 platforms, albeit in opposite directions (downregulated on SomaScan and upregulated on MS). Using the FindMNDBiomarker database, we found that increased CA1 had also been identified in postmortem spinal tissue of ALS and in plasma of bulbar‐ compared with limb‐onset ALS. Interestingly, histological studies have confirmed CA1 expression in human spinal motor neurons where it demonstrates an increased and altered immunoreactive pattern in ALS.
40
Further to this, SOD1G93A transgenic mice administered a CA1 inhibitor show a more rapid decline in motor symptoms and survival,
41
supporting further study into CA1 in ALS pathogenesis. None of the other DEPs identified with SomaScan were found in MS analyses of postmortem tissue or biofluids, indicating low overlap between platforms and the need for future studies to better understand the proteomes detected with newer proteomic platforms.
Comparison of DEPs in plasma and plasma‐derived EVs with proteins altered in the CNS revealed a similar number, although largely different DEPs in plasma EVs and plasma samples. Importantly, most of these proteins have yet to be assessed in ALS, highlighting the need for further investigation into whether plasma EVs better reflect pathological and/or cellular brain changes in ALS. Interestingly, DEPs that consistently emerged in both plasma EVs and plasma included the actin‐binding GSN protein and complement C1QC, the latter having recently been found to be a binding partner of the TREM2 protein,
42
which is expressed on microglia,
43
and interacts with TDP‐43 to protect against TDP‐related neurodegeneration.
44
Specifically, TREM2 was found to bind to C1QC to restrict complement‐mediated synaptic elimination,
42
highlighting the need for further investigation into its involvement in disease pathogenesis, and supporting reproducibility as a means to streamline proteins for further study in ALS pathogenesis.
There are several methodological issues warranting consideration in the current context. Compared with postmortem studies, biofluid studies predominantly involve clinically defined cohorts at an earlier stage of disease. However, this combined analysis enabled us to determine whether proteins identified in a primary region of disease pathology were also detected in peripheral biofluids. We reason that the proteins found to be dysregulated across these two biospecimen types are likely to be an under‐ rather than over‐identification of ALS‐associated changes. In addition to biospecimen type, this analysis included studies in different biospecimen components (eg, plasma, serum, EVs, single‐cells, bulk). Although this allowed us to identify the most consistent protein changes across laboratories/cohorts and explore emerging techniques in the field, future studies in underrepresented biospecimen components are needed to strengthen these findings. Another consideration is interstudy variability in control cohorts (eg, healthy, non‐neurological, or disease controls) and/or variations in proteomic techniques, data processing, and analysis, including statistical approaches and batch effects, which can lead to inconsistent findings that may undermine the robustness of cross‐study findings. Although this may allow for the identification of the most consistent protein changes across diverse technical and biological settings, future efforts to implement standardized pipelines is needed to address this challenge in proteomic research and facilitate reliable meta‐analyses. Finally, studies comparing specific ALS subtypes were limited. As such, although our combined analysis focused on studies in ALS versus controls, we also uploaded the datasets, cohort, and biospecimen details from ALS subtype analyses onto the FindMNDBiomarker database to enable an overview of proteins in the context of disease. For example, a FindMNDBiomarker database search for the 14‐3‐3 protein, YWHAZ, which is localized in healthy Betz cells, but significantly lost with TDP‐43 pathology,
45
reveals that this 14‐3‐3 protein is significantly reduced in spinal tissue at autopsy,
46
but increased in biofluids in bulbar‐ compared with limb‐onset ALS, early‐ compared with late‐onset ALS, and C9‐ALS compared with asymptomatic‐C9 ALS (Table
S3
).

,

As more future studies are conducted, we propose this platform will serve to facilitate comparisons that will determine consistent and unique protein changes that may have been overlooked with current methodologies, and as a resource that helps streamline proteins for further validation and investigation.
In conclusion, the present study presents an accessible database that enables users to quickly position their proteins of interest in the context of other proteomic studies in human ALS biospecimen types. We demonstrate its utility in identifying novel and understudied proteins in ALS, highlighting proteins that are localized in motor neurons with emerging evidence to suggest involvement in ALS pathogenesis. By serving as an accessible compilation of proteomic findings, we propose that FindMNDBiomarker is a resource that will help users prioritize and streamline their proteins of interest for targeted assay development, mechanistic, pathological, and/or further clinical investigation, thereby supporting the discovery of mechanistic drivers and potential biomarkers in ALS.
